lesson.title: The Resolution That Opened the Door to War
lesson.summary: After reported clashes between American and North Vietnamese naval vessels in August 1964, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, granting President Lyndon Johnson sweeping authority to use military force in Vietnam without a formal declaration of war.
lesson.body:
By the early 1960s, the United States had spent more than a decade backing the government of South Vietnam against a communist insurgency supported by North Vietnam, part of the broader Cold War strategy of stopping the spread of communism. Lyndon Johnson, who became president after John Kennedy's assassination in November 1963, inherited that commitment along with a presidency built on an expanding sense of what executive power could accomplish, both at home through the Great Society and abroad through decisive, and largely unchecked, use of military force.

On August 2, 1964, the destroyer USS Maddox, gathering intelligence off the coast of North Vietnam in the Gulf of Tonkin, reported an attack by North Vietnamese torpedo boats. Two nights later, on August 4, the Maddox and a second destroyer, the USS Turner Joy, reported a second attack in darkness and rough seas. Evidence for that second incident was murky at the time and has been widely questioned since, with many historians concluding that no attack actually took place on August 4, likely the result of sonar and radar misreadings during a tense night at sea.

Johnson did not wait for certainty. He asked Congress for authority to respond, and on August 7, 1964, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution by an overwhelming margin, with only two senators, Wayne Morse of Oregon and Ernest Gruening of Alaska, voting against it. The resolution authorized the president to take all necessary measures to repel armed attacks against US forces and to prevent further aggression, without Congress ever issuing a formal declaration of war.

That vague, sweeping language mattered enormously. Johnson and his successor used the resolution as the legal basis for years of escalating military action in Vietnam, treating it as a substitute for a declaration of war that Congress never actually voted on. The episode became a defining example of executive power expansion, showing how a single vote passed in a moment of crisis and incomplete information could hand a president open ended authority to wage a major war, a precedent Congress would later try to rein in during the 1970s.
